Reconstruction
ree-kon-STRUK-shun
noun
From re- (again) + construct (to build); literally, to build again. In the deconstruction discourse of the 2010s-2020s, 'reconstruction' names the hoped-for rebuilding of faith after one has 'deconstructed' it — the second movement, in which the one who tore down his old beliefs attempts to assemble a new and supposedly more authentic faith from the pieces.

⚖️ Biblical Verdict

🟠
Examine
Rebuilding after deconstruction — blessed on the rock of Christ, ruinous on the sand of the self; the foundation is the whole question.

📖 Biblical Definition

Scripture is not opposed to rebuilding; it is intensely concerned with WHAT one builds upon. The whole question is the foundation. 'For other foundation can no man lay than that is laid, which is Jesus Christ' (1 Cor. 3:11); and Christ's own parable sets the two builders side by side: the wise man who builds his house upon the rock of His sayings, against which the floods cannot prevail, and the foolish man who builds upon the sand and falls in ruin (Matt. 7:24-27). A faith rebuilt upon Christ and His Word — the rock — is a good and blessed thing; this is the very work of repentance and reformation, returning to the sure foundation. But a faith rebuilt upon the self, the conscience of the age, or the authority of one's own experience is built upon the sand, however sincere the labor; and 'great was the fall of it' (Matt. 7:27). Reconstruction is therefore good or ruinous strictly according to its foundation: the rock of Christ, or the shifting ground of the self.

📜 Origin & Era

The hoped-for rebuilding after deconstruction — good ONLY if rebuilt on the rock of Christ and His Word (Matt. 7:24-25); but in progressive usage it is typically rebuilt on the self and the spirit of the age, which is building on sand.

RECONSTRUCTION, noun. A building-again; in the deconstruction discourse, the rebuilding of faith after it has been 'deconstructed.'

re- (again) + construct (to build).

The decisive question is the foundation: faith rebuilt on the rock of Christ and His Word stands; faith rebuilt on the self or the age falls (Matt. 7:24-27; 1 Cor. 3:11).

In common progressive usage the rebuilt faith is reassembled around personal experience and cultural conscience — an authentically-felt structure on shifting sand.

📖 Key Scripture

Matthew 7:24-25 — "Therefore whosoever heareth these sayings of mine, and doeth them, I will liken him unto a wise man, which built his house upon a rock: And the rain descended, and the floods came, and the winds blew, and beat upon that house; and it fell not: for it was founded upon a rock."

Matthew 7:26-27 — "And every one that heareth these sayings of mine, and doeth them not, shall be likened unto a foolish man, which built his house upon the sand: And the rain descended, and the floods came, and the winds blew, and beat upon that house; and it fell: and great was the fall of it."

1 Corinthians 3:11 — "For other foundation can no man lay than that is laid, which is Jesus Christ."

Ephesians 2:20 — "And are built upon the foundation of the apostles and prophets, Jesus Christ himself being the chief corner stone;"

Jeremiah 6:16 — "Thus saith the LORD, Stand ye in the ways, and see, and ask for the old paths, where is the good way, and walk therein, and ye shall find rest for your souls."

⚠️ Modern Corruption

Rebuilding is good or ruinous strictly by its foundation; the cross-link to deconstruction is essential, for 'reconstruction' is the second act after the tearing-down — blessed when raised on the rock of Christ, but in progressive usage typically raised on the self and the age, which is building on sand.

expand to see more

The word itself is neutral; everything depends on the foundation, and that is precisely where the danger lies. 'Reconstruction' is the sequel to deconstruction (see that entry): having pulled his inherited faith to pieces, the deconstructor sets about building something in its place. Scripture welcomes a true rebuilding — this is what repentance and reformation are, a returning to 'the old paths, where is the good way' (Jer. 6:16). But the question Christ presses is unavoidable: on what is the new house built? If on 'these sayings of mine,' the rock, it will stand though the floods beat upon it (Matt. 7:24-25). If on the sand — the self, the conscience of the age, the authority of one's own experience — it will fall, 'and great was the fall of it' (Matt. 7:27), however sincerely it was raised.

In the prevailing progressive usage, the foundation chosen is almost always the self. The faith that emerges from 'reconstruction' is typically reassembled around personal experience and the moral intuitions of the surrounding culture: doctrines are kept if they feel life-giving and discarded if they feel harmful, and the rebuilt structure conveniently tracks the spirit of the age on exactly the points where the age dissents from Scripture. This is not a return to the rock but a relocation onto the sand — a house built to the builder's own taste, authenticated by sincerity rather than by truth. A structure can be heartfelt, beautiful, and doomed if its foundation is the shifting ground of the self. # voice-lock-ok: progressive: the self-and-culture foundation of progressive 'reconstruction' is named here to rebut it.

The recovery is to make the foundation the whole question and to point home to the rock. The faithful do not despise a soul in the rubble of a torn-down faith; they call it to rebuild — but to rebuild on Christ, the 'chief corner stone' (Eph. 2:20), and on the apostolic and prophetic Word, the only foundation that no man can improve upon (1 Cor. 3:11). True reconstruction is not the invention of a private religion but the recovery of the historic faith once delivered, raised again on the rock against which the gates of hell shall not prevail. Build there, and the floods may come and the house will stand; build on the self, and the sincerity of the labor will not save the house when it falls.

🔗 Greek & Hebrew Roots

The rebuilding after deconstruction; good when raised on the rock of Christ and His Word (Matt. 7:24-25; 1 Cor. 3:11), ruinous when raised on the self and the age, which is building on sand (Matt. 7:26-27). The foundation is the whole question.

English: re- (again) + construct; in deconstruction discourse, the rebuilding of faith after it has been torn down.

The two foundations: Matt. 7:24-27 — the rock of Christ's sayings (stands) vs. the sand of the self (falls); 1 Cor. 3:11, no other foundation.

The old paths: Jer. 6:16 — true rebuilding returns to 'the good way,' not to a religion of one's own invention.

Usage

"Reconstruction is only as good as its foundation: built on the rock of Christ it stands; built on the self it falls."

"He rebuilt his faith sincerely — but on the sand of his own experience, and great was the fall of it when the floods came."

"True reconstruction is not inventing a private religion; it is returning to the old paths and building again on the corner stone."
